rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Thermal stability in Group IIA is the **polarisation ladder**. The M²⁺ cation bends the big CO₃²⁻/NO₃⁻ electron cloud; polarising power = charge/size, so it falls steadily from Be²⁺ to Ba²⁺. **Carbonates** respond with a clean decomposition-temperature ladder — BeCO₃ <100 °C, MgCO₃ 350 °C, CaCO₃ 900 °C, SrCO₃ 1290 °C, BaCO₃ 1360 °C, all yielding MO + CO₂.…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "The thermal stability of the carbonates of the alkaline earth metals increases with increasing atomic number, because the polarising power of the doubly charged cation decreases as its size increases."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Limestone versus magnesite in the kiln*** — magnesite calcines at 350 °C, limestone demands 900 °C: the same CO₃²⁻ anion, but Mg²⁺ bends it until it snaps while Ca²⁺ merely leans on it — two ores, two kiln temperatures, one Fajans argument.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Why Small Cations Burn Their Carbonates Thermal stability of the Group IIA carbonates and nitrates is the Fajans polarisation story: the smaller the M²⁺ ion, the harder it distorts the big anion's electron cloud, weakening a C–O or N–O bond until CO₂ or NO₂+O₂ escapes.…  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 The decomposition reactions - Carbonates: MCO₃ → MO + CO₂↑ (all except BeCO₃ need heating; BeCO₃ decomposes below 100 °C, MgCO₃ ~350 °C, CaCO₃ ~900 °C, SrCO₃ ~1290 °C, BaCO₃ ~1360 °C). - Nitrates: all decompose on heating, but in two stages of product: - **Be and Mg:** 2M(NO₃)₂ → 2MO + 4NO₂↑ + O₂↑ (nitrate → oxide).…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Carbonate ladder: 100/350/900/1290/1360 C. Nitrate split at Mg/Ca: Be/Mg -> oxide + NO2 + O2; Ca/Sr/Ba -> nitrite + O2. Li parallels Mg (diagonal). Polarising power = charge/size.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Polarising power is charge over size, and it is the single dial that tunes the whole group: the smaller the cation, the more it bends the big anion's cloud, and the lower the temperature at which CO2 or NO2+O2 escapes.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Carbonates MCO3 -> MO + CO2; stability increases down: BeCO3 <100 C, MgCO3 ~350 C, CaCO3 ~900 C, SrCO3 ~1290 C, BaCO3 ~1360 C. Explanation: Fajans polarisation - small M2+ (high charge density) distorts CO3^2-, weakens C-O, anion splits; polarising power = charge/size falls down the group.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ decomposition at ~900 °C releases roughly 0.44 t of CO₂ per tonne of lime — cement kilns are among the world's largest single CO₂ sources, all of it the polarisation ladder's top rung being climbed industrially.

rows.text: Compare the thermal behaviour of Li2CO3 with Na2CO3 and connect it to the Li-Mg diagonal relationship.  ·  ## 6. Common Confusions **"More stable down the group" applies to carbonates AND to the nitrate decomposition *temperature*, but the nitrate *products* change family:** Be/Mg give oxide, Ca/Sr/Ba give nitrite — stability and product identity are different statements.  ·  **NO₂ is brown, O₂ is not:** the decomposition of Mg(NO₃)₂ gives brown fumes (NO₂) plus a colourless gas that relights a glowing splint (O₂) — quote both observations.
